key_insight: Introduce a simple "informative alignment" metric that scores teacher chain-of-thought trajectories by how useful they are for a given student—balancing novelty (informativeness) and learnability (alignment). Selecting trajectories by this metric yields better student reasoning than simply using stronger teachers or by student-likelihood selection.
problem_solved: Data-student suitability: stronger teacher trajectories or those that merely match a student's current behavior do not always produce the best distilled reasoning; we need a way to pick trajectories that the student can actually learn from.
method: Define a lightweight metric that quantifies how informative a teacher trajectory is for a particular student, capturing both corrective signal and how learnable it is.
Score and rank teacher chain-of-thought trajectories with the metric, then select high-scoring trajectories for distillation into the student model.
Empirically compare this selection to baselines (strong-teacher-only, student-likelihood) across reasoning tasks and show improved student performance.
impact: Provides a practical, data-driven selection rule for CoT distillation that improves student LLM reasoning efficiency and final performance, enabling more effective and sample-efficient knowledge transfer during model compression or training.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: multiple teacher CoTs → metric scorer (informative alignment) → selected trajectories → student model
Tradeoff cartoon: novelty/informativeness vs. learnability/alignment illustrating why extremes (too novel or too similar) are suboptimal
Bar chart: student accuracy under different selection strategies (strong teacher, student-likelihood, informative alignment)
Scatter plot: trajectory metric score vs. measured student improvement to show correlation
paper_title: Which Reasoning Trajectories Teach Students to Reason Better? A Simple Metric of Informative Alignment
paper_authors: Yuming Yang, Mingyoung Lai, Wanxu Zhao, Xiaoran Fan, Zhiheng Xi
